title: From Lagaan to Lalkaar: Aamir Khan and Ashutosh Gowarikar Reunite for a Partition-Era Cricket Epic
excerpt: 25 years after their Oscar-nominated classic, the duo team up for a film on legendary cricketer Lala Amarnath — with a script by Rajkumar Hirani and Abhijat Joshi
body:
Key Takeaways
  • Aamir Khan and Ashutosh Gowarikar reunite for the film *Lalkaar*, set in the Partition era.
  • The film focuses on Lala Amarnath, India's first Test centurion, and his cricketing journey.
  • Scripted by Rajkumar Hirani and Abhijat Joshi, known for their successful collaborations.
  • Filming begins in October 2026, with pre-production already underway.
  • This project marks Aamir's return to cricket films after 25 years since *Lagaan*.

Some reunions are fan service. Others feel like destiny wearing a slightly better suit. When word broke today that Aamir Khan and Ashutosh Gowarikar have titled their upcoming reunion *Lalkaar*, the Bollywood corner of the internet did something it rarely does anymore: it got genuinely, unironically excited. And honestly? The excitement is earned. ## The Details According to a Bollywood Hungama scoop, *Lalkaar* is a period sports drama based on the life of Lala Amarnath — India's first Test centurion, the man who walked out to bat for a newly independent nation and made the entire country believe it could compete with the best in the world. The film is set against the volcanic backdrop of the 1947 Partition, which means Gowarikar is once again working in the territory he knows best: sweeping historical drama where personal courage collides with the tectonic forces of history. The script has been written by none other than Rajkumar Hirani and Abhijat Joshi — the duo behind *Munna Bhai*, *3 Idiots*, *PK*, and *Dunki*. That is, arguably, the most commercially successful screenwriting partnership in Hindi cinema history. Their involvement suggests *Lalkaar* is aiming for something that balances emotional accessibility with narrative ambition — the sweet spot where Hirani's filmography has consistently lived. Excel Entertainment — Farhan Akhtar and Ritesh Sidhwani's production house — is bankrolling the project. Filming is scheduled to begin in October 2026, with extensive pre-production already underway. The makers are reportedly searching for a second lead to play Lala Amarnath's closest friend, a character described as the parallel lead. ## Why This Matters Let's start with the obvious. Aamir Khan and Ashutosh Gowarikar last collaborated on *Lagaan* in 2001 — a film that was nominated for the Academy Award for Best Foreign Language Film, that single-handedly proved Indian cinema could tell a sports story with the emotional complexity of a great novel. It remains, a quarter-century later, one of the five or six most important Hindi films ever made. A reunion between them is not a sequel. It is a statement. And the title — *Lalkaar*, which translates roughly to "challenge" or "battle cry" — carries an unmistakable echo of *Lagaan*. "After *Lagaan*, it's time for *Lalkaar*," an industry source told Bollywood Hungama. "The title instils instant recall to their cult, and also promises something new." For Aamir, this is a return to cricket on the big screen after twenty-five years. His recent track record has been uneven — *Laal Singh Chaddha* underperformed, and the public narrative around him has been complicated by personal headlines, including his upcoming wedding to Gauri Spratt on July 5. But Aamir has always been the actor who resets the conversation with one film. If *Lalkaar* is that film, the comeback narrative writes itself. ## The Lala Amarnath Story

For the diaspora audience, Lala Amarnath's story is worth knowing even without a film attached to it. Born in Lahore in 1911, Amarnath scored India's first-ever Test century — against England at Bombay's Gymkhana Ground in 1933, at the age of 21. He went on to captain India in its first Test series against Pakistan in 1952, a politically charged contest that was as much about two nations proving their identity as it was about cricket.His life was marked by extraordinary talent, volcanic temperament, and institutional conflict — he was dropped from the Indian team multiple times despite being its best player, often because he refused to bow to selectors and administrators. He was, in many ways, the original rebel of Indian cricket, a man who played the game on his own terms in an era that demanded deference. That is rich, complicated, inherently cinematic material. It is also the kind of story that connects across borders — the NRI audience in the US and UK, many of whom trace their roots to pre-Partition Punjab, will find personal resonance in a narrative about identity, displacement, and the fierce assertion of belonging through sport. ## The Bigger Picture Aamir Khan is reportedly planning to shoot three films back-to-back starting September 2026, with *Lalkaar* being one of the marquee projects. If that schedule holds, we could see him in an unprecedented burst of productivity after years of deliberate scarcity. For Gowarikar, who has struggled commercially since *Jodhaa Akbar* (2008) despite the critical success of *Panipat* (2019), *Lalkaar* represents a chance to remind audiences why he was once mentioned in the same breath as Sanjay Leela Bhansali and Mani Ratnam. The Hirani-Joshi script gives him a foundation he has not had in years. And for the rest of us? *Lalkaar* is proof that Bollywood still knows how to generate genuine anticipation — not through franchise mathematics or universe-building, but through the old-fashioned promise of great talent meeting great material. *Lagaan* changed what we thought Hindi cinema could be. Twenty-five years later, the same team is betting they can do it again. We will be watching.
